reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: Results from liberation of pigment granules from the posterior iris that deposit throughout the anterior segment and clog the trabecular meshwork, raising intraocular pressure
Typically affects young, myopic adults, more often men, and may be asymptomatic or cause blurring and haloes after exercise or pupillary dilation
A vertical spindle-shaped deposit of pigment on the corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle) is a classic sign
Mid-peripheral radial iris transillumination defects reflect loss of pigment where the iris chafes against the lens zonules
Gonioscopy shows a heavily and homogeneously pigmented trabecular meshwork, often with a concave (posteriorly bowed) peripheral iris
Reverse pupillary block, in which the iris is pushed back against the zonules, is thought to drive the pigment-releasing chafing

Treatment lowers pressure with topical agents; laser peripheral iridotomy may flatten the concave iris and reduce chafing, and laser trabeculoplasty can be effective though it may cause pressure spikes in heavily pigmented angles
Not all patients with pigment dispersion develop glaucoma; the term pigmentary glaucoma applies once pressure-related optic-nerve damage occurs
reference.pathophysiology: In pigment dispersion the peripheral iris bows posteriorly and rubs against the anterior lens zonular bundles during physiological pupil movement, mechanically stripping melanin granules from the posterior iris pigment epithelium. A postulated reverse pupillary block, where aqueous is trapped in the anterior chamber and presses the iris backward, exaggerates this iridozonular contact. Liberated pigment circulates in the aqueous and is deposited on the corneal endothelium as a Krukenberg spindle, on the lens and iris, and within the trabecular meshwork. Accumulated pigment and associated trabecular cell dysfunction reduce aqueous outflow, and in susceptible eyes the resulting rise in intraocular pressure produces glaucomatous optic-nerve damage.
additionalDifferentials: Pigment released by uveitis or intraocular tumour
Pigment dispersion associated with a malpositioned intraocular lens
Pigment liberation after intraocular surgery or laser
additionalInvestigations: Gonioscopy to document dense homogeneous trabecular pigmentation and iris configuration
Slit-lamp examination for a Krukenberg spindle and iris transillumination defects
Applanation tonometry, ideally with post-exercise or post-dilation testing to detect pigment-release pressure spikes
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to assess for glaucomatous damage
Automated perimetry to detect and monitor field loss
Anterior segment imaging to demonstrate the concave peripheral iris where needed
redFlags: Marked pressure spikes after exercise or pupil dilation that can cause acute symptomatic rises
Established optic-nerve cupping and field loss in a young myopic patient
Very high trabecular pigmentation predisposing to exaggerated pressure spikes after laser trabeculoplasty
Progressive damage despite apparently modest baseline pressure
reference.prognosis: Many patients with pigment dispersion syndrome never develop glaucoma, and pigment release often lessens with age as the iris becomes less concave, but those who progress to pigmentary glaucoma can have aggressive pressure elevation in young eyes requiring lifelong monitoring and treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming pigment dispersion syndrome always progresses to glaucoma or, conversely, discharging patients who need long-term surveillance
Missing exercise- or dilation-induced pressure spikes on isolated clinic readings
Applying high-energy laser trabeculoplasty to a heavily pigmented meshwork and provoking a pressure spike
Confusing dense trabecular pigment with pseudoexfoliation material
Overlooking the diagnosis in a young myope with unexplained ocular hypertension
